Q: Again: formatting seconds in std::chrono A:

Your variable now uses std::chrono::system_clock::duaration, which is not seconds.

So in this line, floor is casting to seconds, but assignment to now casts back to nanoseconds.

now = std::chrono::floor<std::chrono::seconds>( now );

You could instead do this, if you want what's printed to have seconds resolution:

std::format( "{0:%H:%M:%S}", std::chrono::floor<std::chrono::seconds>( now ) )

The lesson: Your now and now1 are different types. Only now1 is a type that truncates to seconds.

Q: Boxplot Min/Max Values and Overlaying Points Issues A:

There are some misunderstandings here about what's going on that should be addressed:

  1. It's not that the "error bars" (the whiskers) aren't showing up, it's that the "missing" bars are on top of one of the quartile lines.
  2. The empty white circles are the "fliers", the points that fall outside of the whisker range.
  3. It seems that you're expecting the whiskers to encompass the entire range of the data, when they're instead set up to demarcate the Tukey fences. Those are part of the boxplot, not your later overlay of the points.

I recommend looking at the pyplot documentation for details.

In any case, it sounds like you want your box plots to have bars that correspond to the full range of data. In order to make that happen, change your plt.boxplot call to the following:

plt.boxplot(data, labels=plants, whis=(0, 100))

this sets the bars (i.e. the "whiskers") to go from the 0th to 100th percentiles, i.e. to cover the full range of data.

Here's code to make a similar plot using the Seaborn package and the object oriented pyplot interface. Note that there is no need to set up your data list.

import seaborn as sns
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

## loads a pandas dataframe dataset
## your df can be used in the same way
tips = sns.load_dataset("tips")

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 6))

## create boxplot
medianprops = {"color": "tab:orange"}
sns.boxplot(
    ax=ax,
    data=tips,
    x="day",
    y="total_bill",
    fill=False,
    color="black",
    linewidth=0.5,
    whis=(0.0, 100.0), #type: ignore
    medianprops=medianprops,
)

## create point overlay
sns.stripplot(ax=ax, data=tips, x="day", hue="day", y="total_bill")

## set up axes and title
ax.set_xlabel("Day")
ax.tick_params(axis="x", labelrotation=45)
ax.set_ylabel("Total Bill")
ax.set_title("Total Bill Distribution")

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

Q: When should I use @Transactional and do I still need repository.save() in Spring Boot? A: 
@Service
@RequiredArgsConstructor
public class UserService {

    private final UserRepository userRepository;

    @Transactional
    public void changeUserEmail(Long userId, String newEmail) {
        User user = userRepository.findById(userId)
                .orElseThrow(() -> new EntityNotFoundException("User not found"));

        user.changeEmail(newEmail);     // domain method or direct setter
        // NO save() needed here
    }
}

No, you usually do NOT need repository.save() when:

- the entity was loaded inside the current @Transactional method (or in the same persistence context), and

- you only modify it (setters, domain methods, etc.)

Hibernate's dirty checking will automatically generate and execute the UPDATE on transaction commit.

Calling save() in this situation is redundant (not wrong, but unnecessary).

When do you still need repository.save()?

You do need it (or equivalent) in these cases:

Situation Need save()? Why / what happens
Creating a new entity Yes persist() + INSERT
Entity is detached (JSON, DTO, another thread, session timeout, etc.) Yes triggers merge()
No active transaction Yes no automatic flush otherwise
You need to force flush immediately inside the transaction Sometimes use saveAndFlush() or flush()
You want uniform CRUD style (personal/team preference) Optional many teams keep save() everywhere for readability

Is avoiding save() best practice?

Yes, in 2025/2026 it is considered the cleaner, more idiomatic JPA way for updates of managed entities.

Reasons most experienced teams prefer not calling save() here:

  • Follows JPA persistence context semantics naturally
  • Avoids pointless merge() call (even if it's cheap)
  • Encourages rich domain models (user.changeEmail(), user.activate(), etc.)
  • Prevents the widespread misconception that "you always have to call save to persist anything"

Many recent Spring Data JPA guides, conference talks (Spring I/O, Devoxx, etc.), and popular GitHub projects now explicitly avoid save() on managed updates.

That said: calling save() everywhere is not incorrect, it's just not optimal. Some teams keep it for:

  • visual symmetry in CRUD methods
  • easier search/replace when refactoring
  • junior developers find it less confusing

Does @Transactional improve performance?

No, its primary purpose is correctness (ACID), not speed.

Main goals:

  • Atomicity
  • Consistency
  • Isolation
  • Rollback on error

Nice side effects (performance-related but secondary):

  • Single flush at commit → usually fewer round-trips than auto-commit
  • One persistence context → efficient 1st-level cache
  • @Transactional(readOnly = true) → skips dirty checking + can use lighter queries

But you mainly use @Transactional so your business operation is atomic and consistent — any perf gain is a bonus.

Bottom line => 2026 recommended pattern

@Transactional               ← almost always on service layer
   ↓
findById() / getReferenceById()    ← entity becomes managed
   ↓
modify fields / call domain methods   ← change state
   ↓
let transaction commit                ← dirty checking → UPDATE
   ↓
→ no save() needed for managed updates

Use save() / saveAndFlush() only for:

  • new entities
  • detached entities
  • forcing immediate persistence

Q: Is there a way to insist you should pass a const/string literal to a java method? A:

The usual way to solve this sort of problem is to have some sort of static analysis in your compilation step.

For example, Error Prone offers the CompileTimeConstant annotation & check for this exact issue.
